To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the prevalence of probable pathological gambling in 1996 and 2002 was similar and that the SOGS and CPGI are comparable for screening purposes.

1) the prevalence of probable pathological gamblers in Quebec in 1996 and 2002 did not change significantly, 2) the most common forms of gambling in 2003 were playing lottery tickets, participating in fundraising draws, playing cards, playing bingo, and playing video lotto machines, 3) the South Oaks Gambling screen (SOGS) and the Canadian Problem Gambling index (CPGI) performed equally well when identifying the prevalence of probable problematic gamblers, and

the prevalence of probable pathological gambling in Quebec in 1996 and in 2002 was 1% and 0.8%, respectively, and the discrepancy between the prevalence estimates obtained with screening questionnaires and those obtained with a structured clinical interview was significant.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following 2 issues: the prevalence of pathological gamblers in Quebec and the prevalence of pathological gambler in the province of Quebec.
the prevalence of pathological gaming in the province of Quebec, and the factors that are associated with it.
the prevalence of problem gambling and the characteristics of pathological gamblers in Quebec.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
0.8%, or 1 in 125, of the adult population in Quebec is a pathological gambler.

pathological gambling prevalence in the general population of Quebec in the year 2002 was estimated to be 0.8%, and the most popular gambling activities among the general adult population of Quebec were buying lottery tickets, participating in fundraising draws, gambling in casinos, playing cards with family and friends, playing bingo, and playing video lotto.

0.8 % of the adult population in Quebec in 1996 and in 2002 could be classified as pathological gamblers, based on screening instruments, but that only 0.1% of the adult Quebec population could be classified as having pathological gambling, based on clinical interviews.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of gambling in Quebec has not significantly changed since 1996, despite the decrease in the number of gamblers and the number of hours spent gambling.
the SOGS and CPGI are useful tools to screen for pathological gambling, but they should be used with caution.
the prevalence of gambling problems in Quebec has remained stable over the last 6 years.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SOGS or CPGI should not be used to identify pathological gamblers.
, in the absence of clinical confirmation, the SOGS or CPGI results should be interpreted cautiously.
the prevalence of gambling is decreasing in Quebec, but the prevalence of pathological gamblers remains stable.
